pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Sample preparation for PX-Gal-3 MS-based proteomics Cells scraped on ice were pelleted (500 xg, 3 min, 4°C) and lysed in cold PBS with Branson SFX250 sonicator (15 ms on, 40 ms off, 1 s total on time, 15% amplitude). Protein quantification was performed with DC™ Protein Assay Kit II with a BSA standard curve. Samples were normalized (500 µg, 1 mg/mL) and protein precipitated with methanol (2 mL, O/N, -20°C). Protein was pelleted (3260 xg, 10 min, 4°C) and washed with methanol (1 mL) after sonication to resuspend completely. Protein was pelleted (3260 xg, 10 min, 4°C) then denatured (500 µl 6 M urea in PBS, 10 µl 10% SDS), reduced (50 µl of premixed 200 mM TCEP in PBS and 600 mM K2CO3 in PBS, 30 min, 37°C shaking), and alkylated (70 µl 400 mM iodoacetamide in PBS, 30 min, RT, in dark). Samples were quenched (5.5 mL PBS, 130 µl 10% SDS) then enriched on prewashed streptavidin-agarose beads (1.5 h, RT, rotating). Beads were pelleted (2000 rpm, 2 min, RT) then washed successively with 0.2% SDS in PBS, PBS, and 100 mM TEAB in water (pH 8.5). Beads were transferred to low-bind Eppendorf tubes (Fisher Scientific, 13-698-794) 100 mM TEAB (pH 8.5) and pelleted (2000 rpm, 2 min, RT). Samples were subjected to tryptic digest (2 µg of procine trypsin in 200 µl 100 mM TEAB (pH 8.5), 1 mM CaCl2, O/N, 37°C, shaking). Beads were pelleted (2000 rpm, 5 min, RT) and supernatant carefully retained in new low-bind tube. Beads were washed with 100 µl 100 mM TEAB (pH 8.5) and pelleted (2000, 5 min, RT) to ensure complete transfer of tryptic peptides. Samples were brought to 30% acetonitrile and combined with respective TMT10plex™ Isobaric Label (Thermo Scientific, 90110) (1 h, 37°C, occasional vortex). Reaction was quenched (6 µl 5% hydroxylamine in water, 15 min, RT) and acidified (4 µl formic acid). Samples were dried by vacuum concentration and reconstituted/combined in 5% acetonitrile, 0.5% TFA in water. Samples were desalted with PierceTM Peptide Desalting Spin Columns per manufacturer protocol then dried by vacuum concentration. Samples were stored at -80°C until resuspended in 20 μl of 0.1 % formic acid in water (Buffer A) and loaded onto instrument.  Liquid Chromatography (LC) and synchronous precursor selection (SPS)-MS3 method for proteomics LC was performed with nEasy LC1000 nano liquid chromatography system (Thermo Scientific™) and on-line eluted into a Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer from EASY PepMapTM RSLC C18 column (3% Buffer B – 80% acetonitrile in water, 0.1% formic acid, 10 min hold). Buffer B gradient was adjusted (3 to 38% over 192 min, 38 to 75% over 5 min, 100% hold over 5 min, 100 to 4% over 1 min, 4% hold over 6 min). EASY spray source was set to 50°C and 1.9 kV for ionization (250 nL/min flow). SPS-MS3 scanning (345 to 1500 m/z) at a resolution of 120,000 for MS1 at automatic gain control (AGC) target of 1E5 with maximum injection time of 50 msec was performed in the Orbitrap mass analyzer. Collision-induced dissociation (30% energy) was performed for peptide monoisotopic ions with a charge 2 to 8 and above intensity threshold (5E3) using quadrupole isolation of 1.6 m/z. AGC target of 1.8E4 with maximum injection time of 120 msec was set for ion trap. The dynamic exclusion duration S5 was set to 20 sec with ions excluded after 1 time within +/- 10 ppm mass tolerance. The top ten MS2 ions present between 400 to 1200 m/z were subjected to higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) (65%) for MS3. Orbitrap detection occurred with resolution 50,000 AGC target 1E5, 120 msec injection time, 3 sec specified cycle time for all scan events. Methods were based on Ting et al.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: Quantification and statistical analyses MS-based proteomics experiments were designed with three replicates of 100 nM PX-Gal-3, two replicates of 100 nM PX-Gal-3 with 100 mM lactose, and two replicates of 0 nM PX-Gal-3. Data were processed in Proteome Discoverer v 2.5 (Thermo Scientific™) with the SEQUEST HT homo sapiens sequence database (42,358 proteins). Search allowed for one missed trypsin cleavage site, fixed modifications of carbamidomethyl cysteines and TMT10plex of lysines and N-terminus, and variable modifications of oxidation. Fragment ion mass tolerance was 0.6 Da, and the mass tolerance was 10 ppm with a 1 % FDR. Identified proteins were filtered for greater than or equal to two unique peptides. All keratins were removed from the dataset. GraphPad Prism software was used to perform statistical analysis on quantified proteins with abundance values converted to log2(Y). Statistical comparisons between conditions were performed with an unpaired student’s t test with the average fold change (x-axis) and p-value (y-axis) presented as a volcano plot. Significance was determined for comparisons with a p-value less than 0.05, equating to values greater than 1.30 on the -log(p-value) scale. Two proteomics experiments were performed with the significantly enriched and competed proteins shared by both MS-based proteomics experiments reported with the individual and average enrichment and competition scores (Supplemental Data).

passages.text: Mapping the placental galectin-3 interactome identifies CD9 and ITGB1 as functional glycoprotein counterreceptors during syncytialization
Significance

The fetomaternal interface is laden with glycan-binding proteins (GBPs) and glycoproteins that regulate diverse placental functions. The GBP galectin-3 activates placental syncytialization, but the precise mechanism of galectin-3-mediated fusion is not well-characterized due to inherent challenges of capturing the weak, transient interactions between GBPs and their ligands. To overcome these limitations, we employ a proximity labeling approach, identifying the galectin-3 interactome and distinguishing CD9 and integrin beta 1 among other cell surface glycoproteins as functional counterreceptors. We demonstrate that CD9 glycosylation is required for galectin-3 binding and observe that galectin-3 oligomerization controls glycoprotein organization to promote syncytialization. This work illuminates mechanisms of galectin-3-mediated cell biology and the promise of using proximity tagging to map functional interactions between GBPs and glycoproteins.

The fetomaternal interface is replete with glycan-binding proteins (GBPs) that can interact with cell surface glycoprotein counterreceptors to regulate placental function. Here, we interrogate the role of galectin-3, a GBP that controls placental trophoblast syncytialization, an important differentiation process where progenitor cytotrophoblast cells fuse to produce the multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast. The molecular mechanism of galectin-3-mediated fusion has not yet been elucidated in part due to the difficulty of studying glycan-GBP binding events in live cells. To overcome these challenges, we employ a proximity labeling strategy to identify the galectin-3 interactome. From this interactome dataset, we selected and validated CD9 and integrin beta 1 as functional counterreceptors of galectin-3 and showed that CD9 is glycosylated with an N-linked glycan at a rare noncanonical sequon. Furthermore, we present evidence that galectin-3 acts to physically alter the fluidity of the cellular membrane, and it does not activate canonical syncytialization signaling pathways. Overall, we report that galectin-mediated binding events and their corresponding functions in cell biology can be precisely regulated by select glycoproteins at specific glycosites.

Glycans are posttranslational modifications that affect myriad biological processes like cell recognition, signaling, and differentiation, predominantly through interactions with glycan-binding proteins (GBPs) at the cell surface. The galectin class of GBPs, in particular, are noted for their diverse roles in placental biology. For example, galectin–glycoprotein interactions have been implicated in angiogenesis, immune tolerance, and cell differentiation, all necessary processes for the function of the mature placenta, which must mediate the fetal supply of oxygen and nutrients while shielding the semiallogenic fetus from maternal immune attack and foreign pathogens. These complex functions are distributed among distinct cell types generated by diverging differentiation pathways of progenitor cytotrophoblasts (CTBs). One such terminal differentiation process is syncytialization, the fusion of mononuclear CTBs to create the multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast (STB) layer that composes the outermost perimeter of the placenta. The STB is directly exposed to maternal blood supply and serves as a critical exchange site for nutrients, oxygen, and hormonal signaling across its enhanced surface area. The proper formation of the STB is critical for healthy placentation, as defects are correlated to poor pregnancy outcomes, including placental insufficiency, developmental heart disease, and preeclampsia.

Galectin-3 has been shown to promote the formation of the STB via CTB fusion in cellulo, and reduced fetal and maternal expression of galectin-3 is correlated with placental insufficiency and fetal growth restriction. However, the molecular mechanism of galectin-3-mediated fusion has yet to be elucidated, and the precise glycoproteins engaging galectin-3 for this function have not been identified. While the glycan-binding preferences of galectin-3 toward β-galactoside sugars are well studied, identifying the specific glycoproteins required for binding and function are also key toward comprehensive elucidation of the mechanisms through which galectin-3 controls syncytialization. Furthermore, the elucidation of functional GBP–glycoprotein complexes facilitates the potential for precise targeting of the galectin–glycoconjugate interaction without perturbing global glycosylation or orthogonal galectin interactions. Importantly, the degree of binding and the biological outcome of GBP–glycan interactions can be influenced by the presentation of the glycan on its glycoconjugate carrier, its localization in cells or within plasma membrane microdomains, or its topological orientation relative to the extracellular space. These parameters can be dictated by the protein carrier and its three-dimensional conformation. As such, approaches that neglect the endogenous biological context of GBP ligands or focus solely on the glycome are limited. The identification of GBP interactomes has historically been stymied by insufficient tools that do not capture the transient and relatively weak interactions (KD ~ mM) between GBPs and their ligands in live cells. Indeed, only one placental interactor of galectin-3, solute carrier family 3 member 2 (SLC3A2), has been identified by coimmunoprecipitation. While the interactions between GBPs and their ligands have been previously precluded from study in endogenous contexts due to their chemical and structural complexity, proximity labeling has emerged as a powerful tool to identify the interactions of biomolecules in live cells while preserving the native characteristics of binding.

Our lab has generated a proximity labeling platform to identify the glycan-mediated interactomes of GBPs using recombinant proteins of interest fused with the engineered enzyme APEX2. Upon incubation of APEX2–GBP conjugates with live cells where the GBP can bind to its native counterreceptors, APEX2 catalyzes the formation of short-lived biotin phenoxyl radicals to biotinylate neighboring proteins, effectively converting the weak and dynamic GBP–glycoconjugate interactions to covalent biotin modifications, permitting isolation of tagged proteins through affinity-based streptavidin enrichment and subsequent quantitative mass spectrometry (MS)-based analysis. This method can be applied to live cells, and it can be temporally managed to capture a snapshot of the distribution of galectins and their neighboring proteins. Here, we employ this proximity labeling platform to identify the interactome of galectin-3 in the widely used BeWo cell line model of CTBs to elucidate the mechanism of galectin-3-mediated syncytialization, as well as compare it to forskolin-induced syncytialization. From the putative protein interactors identified by MS-based proteomics, we demonstrate that CD9 and integrin beta 1 (ITGB1) are functional counterreceptors of galectin-3 via CRISPR-Cas9 knockout and antibody blocking. We also identify the site and functional relevance of CD9 N-linked glycosylation and found that this modification occurs at a rare noncanonical sequon. We further demonstrate that through this interaction, galectin-3 inhibits the mobility of CD9 along the cell membrane.
Proximity Labeling Identifies Glycan-Dependent Interactors of Galectin-3.

Exogenous galectin-3 has previously been shown to promote the fusion of CTBs into multinucleated STBs using BeWo cells, a choriocarcinoma cell line used as a model for CTBs (Fig. 1A and SI Appendix, Fig. S1A). We further confirmed that endogenous galectin-3 plays a limited functional role in causing syncytialization, as knockdown models show limited effects on the transcription of canonical syncytialization markers, on phenotypic syncytialization, or the expression of the STB-specific hormone hCGβ (SI Appendix, Fig. S1 B–I). To evaluate whether N-linked glycans or the ability of exogenous galectin-3 to bind glycans contribute to fusion, we assessed galectin-3-mediated fusion in BeWo cells with two modes of glycan perturbation. To alter cellular N-linked glycosylation, we pretreated BeWo cells with kifunensine (10 µg/mL, 48 h), which prevents the addition of the complex β-galactoside motifs recognized by galectin-3 (SI Appendix, Fig. S1J). To inhibit galectin-3 glycan binding, we pretreated galectin-3 with TD139 (15 µM, 15 min), a competitive inhibitor of its carbohydrate recognition domain. After treatment with galectin-3 (48 h), we quantified the number of nuclei in multinucleated cells relative to the total number of nuclei to derive the fusion index, which represents the extent of syncytialization. We observed a significant decrease in the fusion index for both kifunensine-treated BeWo cells and with TD139 pretreatment of galectin-3 (Fig. 1 B and C). These results indicate that both complex N-linked glycans and the ability of galectin-3 to bind these glycans contribute to galectin-3-mediated fusion.

Proximity labeling to identify glycan-dependent galectin-3 interactors. (A) Cartoon depicting the fusion of placental CTBs to multinucleated STBs with galectin-3 treatment. (B) Representative immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy images of BeWo cells after galectin-3 treatment (48 h) show a dose-dependent increase in fusion. Treatment with TD139 (15 µM, 15 min) and kifunensine (10 µg/mL, 48 h) reduces the formation of E-cadherin-negative multinucleated STBs (yellow arrows). (C) Quantification of the fusion index from IF microscopy experiments (B) shows statistically significant reduction in fusion for cells treated with TD139 or kifunensine (n = 3, two independent biological replicates). (D) Cartoon of proximity labeling protocol. The chimeric APEX2-galectin-3 (PX-Gal-3) protein is incubated with live CTBs followed by biotin phenol and H2O2 to biotinylate proximal proteins. Biotinylated proteins can be visualized by IF microscopy, western blot, or enriched with streptavidin beads and subjected to MS-based proteomics. (E) Fluorescence microscopy of cells after PX-Gal-3 proximity labeling shows dose- and glycan-dependent biotinylation. (F) Western blot analysis of cell lysates after PX-Gal-3 proximity labeling confirms dose- and glycan-dependent biotin labeling. (*P ≤ 0.05, **P ≤ 0.01, ***P ≤ 0.001, ****P ≤ 0.0001).

We employed proximity labeling to map the interactome of galectin-3 in BeWo cells (Fig. 1D). Live CTBs were incubated with a recombinant APEX2-galectin-3 (PX-Gal-3) fusion protein and treated with biotin phenol and H2O2. APEX2 catalyzes the formation of biotin phenoxyl radicals that covalently biotinylate proteins proximally located to the galectin-3–glycoprotein complex. Biotinylation was then detected via immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy or western blot analysis to optimize the protocol. For interactome identification, the biotinylated proteins from cell lysates were enriched via streptavidin-agarose beads and prepared for quantitative MS-based proteomics. By fluorescence microscopy, we observed dose-dependent (0 to 100 nM PX-Gal-3) cell surface-localized biotinylation (Fig. 1E). The extent of biotinylation was reduced by the presence of soluble lactose (100 mM), used here as a competitive inhibitor of the carbohydrate binding domain of galectin-3, by pretreatment with kifunensine, or coincubation with TD139, providing further evidence that galectin-3 interactions are glycan-mediated (Fig. 1 E and F and SI Appendix, Fig. S1K). These observations were also validated by western blotting (Fig. 1F and SI Appendix, Fig. S2L) with 100 nM PX-Gal-3 selected as the optimal concentration for MS-based proteomics.

With the optimized conditions, we then performed proximity labeling for MS-based proteomics with tandem mass tagging (TMT) to allow for quantitative comparisons across different conditions. Proximity labeling was performed with PX-Gal-3 (100 nM), PX-Gal-3 (100 nM) coincubated with excess lactose (100 mM), and a no PX-Gal-3 condition as a negative control. Cells were lysed and incubated with streptavidin-agarose beads for enrichment of biotinylated proteins. After washing, beads were subjected to tryptic digestion to release peptides for further preparation. Collected peptides were reduced, alkylated, labeled with tandem mass tags, combined, and desalted before MS-based proteomics. We identified 559 proteins significantly enriched 10-fold over the negative control (Fig. 2A) and 533 proteins significantly enriched fourfold over the competition condition (Fig. 2B). Plotting enrichment vs. competition, we observed a positive correlation (R2 = 0.76) between significantly enriched and competed proteins, suggesting that most interactions are glycan-mediated (Fig. 2C). We observed high correlations between enriched and competed proteins across independent biological replicates (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 A–D). Encouragingly, known galectin-3 interactors were found among the enriched and competed proteins, including SLC3A2, integrins, NOTCH1, EGFR, and the transferrin receptor. We compared the enrichment score of significantly enriched and competed proteins identified by PX-Gal-3 with our previously published cell surface proteome atlas to assess the specificity of PX-Gal-3 labeling and observed limited correlation in these datasets, indicating that the PX-Gal-3 proximity labeling specifically enriches galectin-3 interactors rather than providing a broad survey of the cell surface proteome (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 E and F).

Proximity labeling identifies the galectin-3 interactome in BeWo CTB via MS–based proteomics. (A) Volcano plot of the enriched proteins comparing 100 nM PX-Gal-3 condition relative to a no PX-Gal-3 control. 559 interactors are enriched more than 10-fold over the negative control with statistical significance. (B) Volcano plot of the competed proteins comparing the 100 nM PX-Gal-3 condition relative to 100 nM PX-Gal-3 with 100 mM lactose. 533 proteins are more than fourfold competed with statistical significance. (C) Plot of enrichment vs. competition shows a positive correlation, and 496 proteins are both enriched and competed with statistical significance. Gray dots are not statistically significant and red dots are proteins of interest. (D) Table of proteins of interest selected for further experiments and their average enrichment and competition score across two independent biological replicates. (E) STRING analysis of the 25 most enriched proteins from two MS-based proteomics experiments shows CD9 and ITGB1 as central nodes.

To select candidate proteins for further validation (Fig. 2D), we subjected the 25 proteins with the highest enrichment score averaged across the two experiments to STRING network analysis. We found CD9 and ITGB1 to be central nodes of the network (Fig. 2E). Because CD9 is a tetraspanin implicated in muscle regeneration and myogenesis (a fusion process analogous to syncytialization), sperm/egg cell fusion, and galectin-3-independent syncytialization, we hypothesized that it could play a functional role in galectin-3-mediated fusion. Further, ITGB1 is known to associate with CD9, including at cell–cell contact sites, and it is known to modulate CD9 activation. Thus, we prioritized both CD9 and ITGB1 as targets for functional studies. We performed DAVID analysis of the “Biological Process” gene ontology (GO) annotations of the significantly enriched and competed cell surface proteins, and found recurrence of INSR and IGF1R (indicated with*) for GO terms affecting cellular responses critical to syncytialization (SI Appendix, Fig. S2G). Because the interaction between galectin-3 and INSR has previously been shown to drive insulin resistance through perturbed signaling, we hypothesized this interaction could crosstalk with syncytialization-associated signaling cascades. We also selected neural cell adhesion molecule 1 (NCAM1), which is transcriptionally upregulated in myogenesis and known to improve myoblast differentiation when overexpressed.
Galectin-3 Interacts with CD9 and ITGB1 to Promote Fusion.

To determine whether interactions between PX-Gal-3 and the candidate glycoproteins were mediated by glycans, we performed an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) and observed lactose-competed binding events, suggesting these interactions were likely glycan-mediated (SI Appendix, Fig. S3A). To assess whether these interactions functionally contributed to syncytialization, we generated single-clone CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts of CD9, ITGB1, NCAM1, IGF1R, and INSR, as well as a scramble guide RNA (scr) control (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 B–D), and treated these cell lines with increasing concentrations of galectin-3 (0 to 40 µg/mL). We observed abrogation of galectin-3-mediated fusion only with CD9KO and ITGB1KO BeWo cells compared to wild-type (WT) and scr BeWo cells, suggesting that these proteins could serve as functional counterreceptors for fusion (Fig. 3 A and B and SI Appendix, Fig. S3F).

Functional validation of CD9 and ITGB1 as counterreceptors in galectin-3-mediated CTB fusion. (A) Representative IF microscopy images of WT, scramble guide (scr), CRISPR-Cas9 CD9KO, and ITGB1KO BeWo cell lines treated with vehicle and 40 µg/mL galectin-3. (B) Quantification of the fusion index experiment (A) shows that CD9KO and ITGB1KO are the only mutants with statistically significant impairments in fusion index (n = 3, two independent biological replicates). (C) Representative IF microscopy images for antibody blocking (10 µg/mL, 4 h pretreatment) of galectin-3-mediated fusion. (D) Quantification of fusion index experiment (C) shows blocking of CD9 and ITGB1 reduces fusion index relative to no antibody and IgG isotype control (n = 6, two independent biological replicates). (E) Quantification of biotinylation after PX-Gal-3 proximity labeling (F) shows statistically significant reduction in biotinylation in cells lacking CD9 and/or ITGB1 (two independent biological replicates). (F) Representative western blot image of proximity labeling with PX-Gal-3 in WT, CD9KO, ITGB1KO, and CD9KOITGB1KD cells. (*P ≤ 0.05, **P ≤ 0.01, ***P ≤ 0.001, ****P ≤ 0.0001. Relevant nonsignificant differences are indicated with n.s.)

Based on these observations, we narrowed our focus toward CD9 and ITGB1. We performed antibody blocking experiments where BeWo cells were pretreated (10 µg/mL, 4 h, 37 °C) with an anti-CD9 antibody, an anti-ITGB1 antibody, or an isotype IgG control before treating with vehicle or galectin-3 (40 µg/mL). We observed that CD9 and ITGB1 blocking reduced the fusion index of galectin-3-treated cells compared to the untreated and isotype controls (Fig. 3 C and D). To determine whether galectin-3 engagement to cells is affected by the loss of CD9, ITGB1, or of both proteins, we generated single (CD9KO, ITGB1KO) or double knockdown (CD9KOITGB1KD) clones and observed that proximity tagging with PX-Gal-3 was significantly decreased in both single knockout and double knockdown clones by probing for biotinylated proteins (Fig. 3 E and F). These results suggest that both CD9 and ITGB1 are direct functional interactors of galectin-3 in BeWo cells.
Galectin-3 Does Not Activate Canonical Syncytialization Signaling Pathways.

We sought to further explore the mechanism of galectin-3-mediated fusion, probing both biophysical and biochemical functions. Galectin-3 can multimerize through its disordered N-terminal domain to generate a galectin lattice that can affect counterreceptor localization, clustering, and propensity to endocytose. Due to the dependence of many glycan-mediated interactions on multivalency, we posited that artificial multimers of galectin-3 would more effectively promote fusion than monomeric galectin-3. We compared the fusion indices of BeWo cells treated with WT galectin-3 or with engineered valence-restricted constructs of galectin-3 in the monomeric (G1), trimeric (G3), and hexameric states (G6). We observed that treatment with multimeric galectin-3 (G3 and G6) increased fusion index similarly to WT galectin-3, whereas monomeric galectin-3 did not increase the fusion index (Fig. 4 A and B). These results support a model in which galectin-3 promotes placental cell fusion by oligomerizing to bind to N-glycosylated counterreceptors.

Galectin-3 oligomerization regulates CTB fusion but does not activate the canonical signaling pathways involved in syncytialization. (A) Representative IF microscopy images of BeWo cells treated with increasing doses of galectin-3 with different valency (G1 – monomeric, G3 – trimeric, G6 – hexameric). (B) Quantification of the fusion index experiment (A) shows that G1 does not promote fusion, while G3 and G6 are equivalent to WT (n = 3, two independent biological replicates). (C) RT-qPCR of syncytialization markers (SYN1, SYN2, GCM1, CGB) in cells treated with vehicle (DMSO, PBS), forskolin (FK, 20 µM, 48 h), or galectin-3 (Gal-3, 40 µg/mL, 48 h) (n = 3, three independent biological replicates). (D) Representative IF images of hCGβ expression in forskolin and galectin-3 treated cells (48 h). (E) Western blot of hCGβ secreted in the media after treatment (48 h) with forskolin or galectin-3. (F) Measurement of cAMP in BeWo cells after treatment with forskolin or galectin-3 (15 min) (two independent biological replicates). (*P ≤ 0.05, **P ≤ 0.01, ***P ≤ 0.001, ****P ≤ 0.0001). Relevant nonsignificant differences are indicated with n.s.)

Because galectin-3 can also modulate signaling, we next tested whether galectin-3 treatment induced the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)-related canonical syncytialization pathways upregulated by forskolin treatment (SI Appendix, Fig. S4 A and B). We measured the expression of syncytialization markers (SYN1, SYN2, CGB, and GCM1) in galectin-3-treated BeWo cells and forskolin-treated positive control BeWo cells. Transcripts of syncytialization markers increased with statistical significance with forskolin treatment relative to the negative control (Fig. 4C). However, galectin-3 treatment did not affect SYN1, SYN2, and CGB transcript levels, only increasing the transcript level of GCM1 by 20% (compared to nearly 100% increase with forskolin treatment) (Fig. 4C). We also measured the production of the STB-specific hormone hCGβ by IF microscopy (Fig. 4D), western blot analysis (Fig. 4E and SI Appendix, Fig. S4C), and quantitative ELISA (SI Appendix, Fig. S4D). We observed increases in cellular and secreted hCGβ with forskolin treatment relative to the negative control but no difference with galectin-3 treatment. These observations are consistent with those of galectin-1 (another member of the galectin family), which is reported to promote fusion of CTBs without inducing the expression of hCGβ. Using a cell-based ELISA, we observed a statistically significant, dose-dependent increase of cAMP (which initiates the syncytialization signaling cascade) in forskolin-treated BeWo cells but not with galectin-3 treatment (Fig. 4F and SI Appendix, Fig. S4 E and F). These results indicate that while galectin-3 promotes fusion of BeWo cells in the CTB state, the resultant multinucleated STBs do not display the canonical markers of syncytialization measured in forskolin-treated cells. These results suggest that galectin-3 could promote BeWo fusion through a noncanonical signaling pathway to induce fusion and/or act biophysically to alter membrane dynamics. Together, galectin-3 and cAMP-related signaling pathways may be responsible for proper trophoblast syncytialization in vivo.
Characterization of CD9 Glycosylation at Rare Noncanonical N-X-C Glycosite.

To evaluate the role of CD9 glycosylation in its interaction with galectin-3, we characterized the site of CD9 glycosylation. While CD9 has been classified as a glycoprotein, the site of glycosylation has only been predicted, not empirically validated, and there are conflicting reports of CD9 glycosylation, where some cell types (e.g., MEC and SNU878) do not express the glycosylated form. We observed in BeWo cells that both endogenous and overexpressed CD9 appear as two discrete bands by western blotting (SI Appendix, Fig. S5A). Upon treatment of lysates with PNGase F, an amidase that cleaves glycans from N-linked glycoconjugates, we observed a collapse of the two bands to one at the lower molecular weight (SI Appendix, Fig. S5A). This observation suggests that the higher molecular weight band is N-linked glycosylated CD9 (representing approximately 10% of endogenously expressed CD9 and 40% of overexpressed CD9 by western blot densitometry), and the lower band corresponds to nonglycosylated CD9. CD9 glycosylation was also observed in the HTR-8/SVneo trophoblast cell line and human placental lysates from normal pregnancies (SI Appendix, Fig. S5 B–D), suggesting the biological relevance of N-linked glycosylated CD9 beyond BeWo cells.

N-linked glycosylation canonically occurs at the asparagine residue of N-X-S/T sequons, in which X can be any residue except for proline. Therefore, it has been assumed that CD9 is glycosylated at either N52 or N53 of the small extracellular loop, as both residues are part of this sequon (Fig. 5A). We transiently overexpressed conservative N52Q, N53Q, and N52,53Q mutants to determine which of these two sites could be modified by N-linked glycans. However, the presence of the higher molecular weight band persisted in the mutants (Fig. 5A). We hypothesized that the unusual appearance of four asparagine residues in a sequence may allow for position N50 or N51 to be glycosylated to compensate for the absence of N52 or N53 glycosylation. However, even with all four consecutive asparagine residues mutated, CD9 remained glycosylated (Fig. 5A and SI Appendix, Fig. S5E). While N-linked glycosylation outside the canonical N-X-S/T sequon is relatively rare, we systematically tested the remaining three extracellular asparagine residues of CD9 and found that N151Q was the only nonglycosylated mutant appearing as a single band (Fig. 5B and SI Appendix, Fig. S5E). This residue is part of an unusual N-X-C sequon, empirically validated in only a handful of proteins, such as plasma protein C, von Willebrand factor, SPINT2, and CD69, and predicted to represent less than 3% of all N-linked glycosites across the proteome. Mutation of the cysteine residue of this N-X-C sequon to alanine also prevented CD9 glycosylation (SI Appendix, Fig. S5F), suggesting that the presence of the cysteine residue is key toward N-linked glycosylation. To confirm glycan occupancy on endogenous CD9, we immunoprecipitated CD9 from BeWo cell lysates and subjected digested peptides to deglycosylation with PNGase F treatment in O18 water. This process causes a signature N+3 mass modification on an N-glycosylated asparagine residue. We identified CD9 peptides mapping to position N151, with and without the N+3 signature mass modification, suggesting this site exists both in a glycosylated and nonglycosylated state (SI Appendix, Fig. S6 A and B). We did not observe any N+3 modifications at peptides mapping to N50-53, suggesting CD9 glycosylation does not occur at these sites. These results corroborate our findings from mutational analysis that CD9 is glycosylated at N151, representing approximately 10% of total endogenous CD9 protein.

We performed a BLAST search comparing human CD9 to other species to see whether the N151 glycosylation site was conserved. Whereas some mammals like gorillas and bats possess the cognate N-X-C sequon, we found that many mammalian species, including mice, have an aspartate residue instead of asparagine (SI Appendix, Fig. S7A). We mutated this aspartate to asparagine and observed neo-glycosylation in overexpressed murine CD9 (SI Appendix, Fig. S7 B and C). This result suggests that this noncanonical N-X-C sequon is specifically recognized as a glycosylation site in the large extracellular loop of CD9. This site topologically places the glycan more distal to the membrane and in a more flexible portion of CD9 than the predicted small extracellular loop glycosylation site, likely increasing the accessibility of the glycan to GBP interactors. This finding enabled the generation of CD9 glycosite mutant control constructs for subsequent experiments.
Galectin-3/CD9 Functional Interaction Is Dependent on Glycosylation.

With the N-linked glycosite identified, we then assessed the glycosylation-dependent impact of galectin-3 on CD9 membrane dynamics. We measured the diffusion coefficient (D) of mCherry-tagged CD9 (mCherry-CD9) and mCherry-CD9N151Q (SI Appendix, Fig. S8A) over 24 h following treatment with increasing concentrations of galectin-3 (0 to 40 µg/mL) via Imaging Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy. In the absence of galectin-3, mCherry-CD9 displayed stable diffusion coefficients throughout the experiment (SI Appendix, Table S1). In contrast, mCherry-CD9 exhibited a significant and time-dependent decrease in diffusion coefficient upon galectin-3 treatment, with the effect being more pronounced at higher concentrations with an 18.8% reduction in D at the highest concentration (Fig. 5 C and D). To quantitatively describe the time-dependent reduction in mCherry-CD9 diffusion upon galectin-3 treatment, we applied logistic fitting to extract key transition parameters, including the rate constant (k) and the half-transition time (t1/2), which represents the time at which half of the total diffusion reduction occurs (SI Appendix, Table S2). We observed that as galectin-3 concentration increased, the transition time t1/2 significantly decreased and the rate constant increased, indicating a more rapid immobilization of mCherry-CD9 at higher concentrations of galectin-3. This effect was exclusive to galectin-3-mediated fusion, as forskolin treatment did not reduce mCherry-CD9 D (SI Appendix, Fig. S8D) In contrast, mCherry-CD9N151Q showed minimal changes in D across all galectin-3 concentrations and time points, suggesting a lack of interaction between the CD9 glycosite mutant and galectin-3 (Fig. 5 E and F). Further, mCherry-CD9N151Q exhibited minimal changes in the kinetic parameters measured across all concentrations tested (SI Appendix, Table S2). These findings suggest that galectin-3 treatment restricts CD9 mobility across the plasma membrane in a concentration-dependent manner, with higher concentrations inducing a more pronounced and sustained reduction in diffusion. To determine whether the observed effect on diffusion was due to a direct interaction between CD9 and galectin-3, we performed colocalization experiments with galectin-3 and the WT or N151Q mCherry-CD9 constructs by confocal microscopy (Fig. 5G). We observed a twofold increase in the overlap between galectin-3 and WT CD9 compared to the glycosite mutant (Fig. 5 H and I and SI Appendix, Table S3). Both the colocalization and progressive decline in CD9 diffusion over time suggests that galectin-3 directly promotes clustering or confinement of CD9 within specific membrane domains, leading to a reduced lateral diffusion profile. The lack of response to galectin-3 treatment with mCherry-CD9N151Q suggests that glycosylation at N151 is essential for galectin-3 binding and its subsequent effects on CD9 mobility. The absence of glycosylation likely disrupts galectin-3-induced clustering or confinement of CD9, allowing CD9 N151Q to maintain its original diffusion dynamics regardless of galectin-3 treatment. These results are consistent with reports of other tetraspanin–galectin interactions affecting membrane organization.

To determine whether CD9 glycosylation is also necessary for galectin-3-mediated fusion, we created cell lines stably expressing WT CD9 and CD9 N151Q in WT, scr, and CD9KO BeWo cells (SI Appendix, Fig. S8 B and C). We then treated these cell lines with vehicle or galectin-3 (40 µg/mL, 48 h) and measured the fusion index. CD9KO cells expressing WT CD9 achieved a statistically significant and nearly complete rescue of the fusion index (~80% relative to WT BeWo cells), whereas CD9KO cells expressing mutant CD9 N151Q could not achieve rescue and were not statistically different than nontransduced or empty vector-transduced CD9KO controls (Fig. 5 J and K and SI Appendix, Fig. S8 E and F). These results suggest that CD9 glycosylation is necessary for galectin-3-mediated fusion of BeWo cells and supports our model in which galectin-3 oligomerizes and binds to the glycans on CD9 to affect cell fusion.
Discussion

The interactions between GBPs and their glycoconjugate counterreceptors mediate important biological processes, but these interactions can be difficult to elucidate in living cells. GBPs generally exhibit avidity for their counterreceptors, and while these interactions can be measured in vitro, the biological context of a living cell is necessary to determine whether an interaction can exhibit a functional phenotypic outcome. In this work, we demonstrate that APEX2-based proximity tagging represents an effective strategy to identify galectin-3 counterreceptors in placental trophoblasts and use network analyses to parse and prioritize glycoproteins (e.g., CD9 and ITGB1) for functional validation. Hence, binding-first approaches, like proximity tagging, nicely complement genetic screens for the identification of functional GBP counterreceptors. We also note the enhanced sensitivity of the proximity tagging protocol in detecting changes in GBP engagement relative to “binding-only” approaches, which required >10-fold higher probe concentrations for detection (SI Appendix, Fig. S9 A and C).

The identification of galectin-3 functional counterreceptors was leveraged to reveal mechanistic insight into galectin-3-mediated fusion. Whereas both fetal and maternal serum galectin-3 are important for proper placental formation in vivo, exogenous treatment of galectin-3 is necessary to stimulate fusion in BeWo cell models. Indeed, histological staining of placental tissues, where galectin-3 expression is minimal in STBs but high in CTB, extravillous trophoblasts, and the maternal decidua, represents multiple putative sources of exogenous galectin-3. We demonstrate that galectin-3-mediated BeWo fusion is dependent on glycosylation, the galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain, and the oligomerization state of galectin-3. These results support a model where galectin-3 lattice formation is important for fusion. We also compared galectin-3-mediated syncytialization to forskolin-mediated syncytialization and show that, similar to galectin-1, galectin-3 does not increase the expression of the STB marker hCGβ. Additionally, the canonical syncytialization signaling pathways are not activated by galectin-3, but we do observe an immobilizing effect on CD9 membrane protein diffusion with galectin-3 treatment to a similar degree as other work examining CD9 dynamics. Further studies will need to be performed to determine whether galectin-3 activates a noncanonical signaling pathway through its interaction network or biophysically promotes fusion, potentially generating “pseudosyncytiotrophoblasts” instead of completely differentiating the CTBs.

Our investigations led us to the finding that CD9 N-linked glycosylation occurs at a noncanonical N-X-C sequon in the large extracellular loop instead of at N-X-S/T sequons present in the small extracellular loop. We validate and characterize this glycosite via mutagenesis. There are two instances of CD9 glycosylation at position N151 present in large glycoproteomics datasets, which were not previously validated or further explored. Interestingly, the N151 position of CD9 is similar to the glycosylation site of all other human tetraspanins (except for the nonglycosylated tetraspanin CD81), suggesting a conserved structural or functional role of this glycosite. Glycosylation at N-X-C sequons has been hypothesized to affect protein folding and disulfide bridge formation. Interestingly, the two cysteines succeeding this glycosite in CD9, C152, and C153, have been shown to participate in disulfide bond formation with C181 and C167, respectively. Thus, the effect of N151 glycosylation on CD9 protein structure and folding warrants further study. Additionally, CD9 protein–protein interactors (such as ITGB1) are believed to be mediated by the large extracellular loop. We speculate that CD9 glycosylation state could regulate these interactions, dictating the proximal protein neighborhood of CD9 and subsequent function. Finally, because the N151 glycosite is not conserved across all mammals, there could be important evolutionary implications of CD9 glycosylation in its various functional roles. Our identification of the CD9 glycosite allows for future experimentation to consider its glycosylation in other contexts, such as in immunology or cancer biology.

In summary, we present evidence that galectin-3 promotes placental cell fusion through a mechanism unique from forskolin, and it does so through interactions with glycosylated CD9 and the glycoprotein ITGB1. CD9 has been implicated in physically affecting membrane architecture, including acting as a sensor of membrane curvature, localizing to stretched membranes during cell shape remodeling. Thus, we speculate that galectin-3 may reorganize the membrane to cluster CD9, potentially inducing membrane bending at sites of high CD9 density. This work was performed in the BeWo choriocarcinoma cell line model of CTB, and other, more complex models, like spontaneously differentiating primary human trophoblasts, may also exhibit these functional relationships. By contributing to the understanding of how galectin-3 treatment affects CTB unable to differentiate without exogenous activation, we can now examine the effect of galectin-3 treatment on models with spontaneous syncytialization to determine whether galectin-3 additively contributes to primary trophoblast fusion.
Materials and Methods
Proximity Labeling and MS-Based Proteomics.

Live cells were washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) followed by PX-Gal-3 incubation (varying concentrations, 30 min, 37 °C) in serum-free culture medium. PX-Gal-3 was preincubated with lactose (100 mM) or TD139 (15.4 µM) (15 min, RT) for competition conditions. Cells were washed with PBS three times and then incubated with biotin phenol (500 µM, 30 min, 37 °C) in serum-containing culture medium. H2O2 was directly added (final 1 mM, 1 min, RT) to label cells followed by three washes with quencher solution. Cells were washed once with PBS, then scraped, and pelleted on ice for lysate-based experiments or fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for microscopy-based experiments. For MS-based proteomics, samples were lysed with a probe sonicator, and lysates were normalized before precipitation with methanol. Protein was washed with methanol, denatured (6 M urea in PBS, 0.2% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)), reduced (200 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP) and 600 mM K2CO3 in PBS, 30 min, 37 °C shaking), and alkylated (400 mM iodoacetamide in PBS, 30 min, RT, in dark). Samples were enriched on prewashed streptavidin-agarose beads (1.5 h, RT, rotating) and washed successively with 0.2% SDS in PBS, PBS, and 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) in water (pH 8.5). Samples were subjected to tryptic digest [2 µg of procine trypsin in 200 µL 100 mM TEAB (pH 8.5), 1 mM CaCl2, O/N, 37 °C, shaking], brought to 30% acetonitrile, and combined with respective TMT10plex™ Isobaric Label (Thermo Scientific, 90110) (1 h, 37 °C, occasional vortex). Reaction was quenched (6 µL 5% hydroxylamine in water, 15 min, RT) and acidified (4 µL formic acid). Samples were dried by vacuum concentration and reconstituted/combined in 5% acetonitrile, 0.5% TFA in water. Samples were desalted with Pierce™ Peptide Desalting Spin Columns per manufacturer protocol and then dried by vacuum concentration. Samples were stored at −80 °C until resuspended in 20 μL of 0.1% formic acid in water (Buffer A) and loaded onto instrument. Subsequent liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) and analysis are described in detail in SI Appendix.
Fusion Index Measurements.

Fixed cells were incubated with primary anti-E-cadherin (1:500, 2% BSA in phosphate-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween 20 (PBST), 4 °C, overnight), washed three times with PBST, incubated with secondary anti-rabbit-647 (1:1,000, 2% BSA in PBST, 1 h, RT), incubated with Hoechst (1:1,000, PBST, 10 min, RT), washed three times with PBST, and then imaged with the EVOS microscope system. Images were analyzed in Fiji (2.14.0) to determine total nuclei count. Briefly, a binary color system was applied to the Hoechst channel followed by a watershed to demarcate nuclei that may be touching. Particles were then counted with a size threshold of at least 200 square pixels. The number of nuclei in syncytia was then determined by counting the nuclei that lacked clear surface E-cadherin staining or cells with a clear border of E-cadherin containing more than one nucleus. Fusion index was derived by dividing number of nuclei in syncytia by the total number of nuclei and reported relative to WT BeWo cells treated with 40 µg/mL galectin-3.
Transfections, Transductions, and siRNA-Mediated Knockdown.

Transient transfections were performed with Lipofectamine 3000 (ThermoFisher) per the manufacturer’s recommendations. Viral production was performed by transfecting HEK293T cells (seeded in 10 cm2 dish, 3 × 106 cells) with 5 µg vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein (VSV-G), 7.5 µg psPAX2, 10 µg of vector of interest, and 67.5 µL FuGENE HD (Promega, E2312) complexed in 1 mL of Optimem (15 min, RT). Medium was changed 6 h later, replenished with 5 mL of culture medium, and then harvested (60 h). For viral transduction, BeWo cells (4 × 105 cells) were seeded in a 6-well plate and allowed to adhere overnight in culture medium. Cells were then spinoculated with 1 mL of harvested viral media (2,000 rpm, 2 h, 37 °C) and underwent antibiotic selection (concentration previously determined in our hands by kill curve) after recovery in culture medium. For small interfering ribonucleic acid (siRNA)-mediated knockdown, BeWo cells were reverse transfected at time of seeding using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (ThermoFisher) per the manufacturer’s protocols.
RNA Extraction and RT-qPCR.

Cells were washed twice with PBS, harvested with 0.25% trypsin (10 min, 37 °C), and pelleted (500× g, 3 min). After one PBS wash, RNA was extracted using the Direct-zol RNA Miniprep kit (Zymo, R2053) per manufacturer instructions. RNA concentration was determined with the NanoDrop OneC. RNA was normalized to less than 200 ng/µL and complementary DNA (cDNA) generated with the Applied Biosystems™ High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit per manufacturer protocol. RT-qPCR was performed with 5 ng cDNA and 500 nM primers using the PowerUp™ SYBR™ Green Master Mix per manufacturer instructions using the QuantStudio™ 6 Pro Real-Time PCR System instrument. GAPDH served as the internal control for analysis.
Microscopy.

Live cell microscopy experiments were performed with a Nikon total internal reflection fluorescence and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (TIRF/STORM) microscope equipped with an oil immersion objective (PlanApo, 100×, NA 1.49; Leica Microsystems, Germany), a 561 nm a high power LUNV laser, and a Hamamatsu Orca Flash 4 CMOS camera. Briefly, a stack of 40,000 images from a region of interest (ROI) on the ventral plasma membrane was recorded at an acquisition speed of 6.2 ms/frame using the TIRF microscope and cMOS camera described above and saved as .ND2 file. The ROI size for cells was 100 × 100 pixels with a pixel size of 60 nm in the object plane. Raw temporal autocorrelation function (G(τ)) was computed from each 4 × 4 binned pixels (Px unit; length = 2.4 nm) of an image stack and fitted with equation 1. For confocal microscopy, two-color confocal imaging was performed using a Zeiss LSM 880 laser scanning confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) equipped with a Plan-Apochromat 63× oil-immersion objective (NA 1.4). GFP was excited with the 488-nm line of an argon laser, and emission was collected using a 500 to 550 nm band-pass filter. mCherry was excited with the 561-nm line of a diode-pumped solid-state laser, and emission was collected using a 580 to 650 nm band-pass filter. Channels were acquired sequentially to avoid bleed-through, with laser power and detector gain optimized for each fluorophore while maintaining identical pixel size (0.07 µm/pixel) and precise spatial registration between channels. For each fluorescence channel, bright spots were detected and counted on a per-cell basis using the Find Maxima function in Fiji (2.14.0). Two spots, one from each channel, were considered overlapping when their centroid positions were within 2 pixels (0.14 µm) of each other.
Immunoblotting.

Normalized lysates were boiled in 1× Laemmli Buffer, 10% β-mercaptoethanol and ran with Tris-Glycine extended shelf life-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (TGX-PAGE) gels (Bio-Rad). Gels were transferred to PVDF membranes using the Trans-Blot Turbo Transfer system (Bio-Rad) per manufacturer protocols. Blots were blocked with 5% BSA in TBST (1 h, RT, rocking), incubated with primary antibodies (O/N, 4 °C, rocking, dilutions in SI Appendix, Table S9), washed with TBST, and incubated with secondary antibodies (1 h, RT, rocking, dilutions in SI Appendix, Table S9). Blots were washed again before imaging with the ChemiDoc imaging system (Bio-Rad).
CD9 IP-MS.

Briefly, CD9 was immunoprecipitated with protein A/G beads (Rockland) crosslinked in-house with anti-CD9 antibody (Abcam, ab236630). BeWo cells were lysed in cold lysis buffer with protease inhibitor cocktail while incubating on ice (50 mM Tris, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), pH 7.5, and 0.5% Igepal CA-630, 20 min), then sonicated (3 min, RT), preclarified (16,000× g, 30 min, 4 °C), and precleared with unmodified protein A/G beads (2 h, 4 °C, rotating). Precleared lysate was then transferred to antibody-crosslinked protein A/G beads (O/N, 4 °C, rotating). Beads were washed with cold lysis buffer three times, cold wash buffer twice (50 mM Tris, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 7.5), and eluted (200 mM glycine, pH 2.3, 0.5% Igepal CA-630, 20 min, 37 °C, shaking). Eluate was neutralized (20% v/v with 1 M tris buffer, pH 8.0) and then prepared for MS-based glycoproteomics through denaturation, alkylation, enzymatic digestion, and PNGase F treatment in H218O. Subsequent LC–MS/MS and analysis are described in detail in SI Appendix.
